---
title: "M covariate slopes with AR1 residuals"
output:
  html_document:
    self_contained: true
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6, dpi = 120,
  fig.path = "results/m_random_slopes/figures/")
result <- readRDS("results/m_random_slopes/recovery.rds")
runs <- result$runs
parameters <- result$parameters
label <- c(informative = "Eight groups", four_groups = "Four groups",
  persistent = "Persistent covariate/residuals")
performance <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(runs, interaction(runs$scenario, runs$kind)), function(x) {
  data.frame(Scenario = label[x$scenario[1]], Experiment = x$kind[1],
    Attempts = nrow(x), Converged = sum(x$is_converged),
    `Positive Hessian` = sum(x$pdHess), Errors = sum(nzchar(x$error)),
    `Median gradient` = median(x$gradient, na.rm = TRUE), check.names = FALSE)
}))
summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(parameters,
  interaction(parameters$scenario, parameters$kind, parameters$parameter)), function(x) {
    available <- x$pdHess & is.finite(x$lower) & is.finite(x$upper)
    data.frame(scenario = x$scenario[1], kind = x$kind[1], parameter = x$parameter[1],
      truth = x$truth[1], median = median(x$estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
      bias = median(x$estimate - x$truth, na.rm = TRUE),
      intervals = sum(available),
      coverage = if (any(available)) mean(x$lower[available] <= x$truth[available] &
        x$upper[available] >= x$truth[available]) else NA_real_)
}))
```

## What is being enabled?

An age group can have its own response to a supplied food or environmental
covariate, with differences between groups partially pooled toward a common
slope. AR1 deviations describe the remaining mortality variation.

```{r specification, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
M_settings = list(process = "ar1", mu_supplied = ~ I(.3),
  mu_form = ~ 0 + capelin + iid(M_age_group, by = capelin))
```

This is a narrow extension. M blocks still share **actual mortality**, so
every mean component must agree within each block. Separate slope groups
cannot split a shared state. A coarser slope grouping may span several M
blocks. `mean_ages` changes reported averages, not the ages receiving a slope.

The model is

\[
\log M_{t,b}=\log(0.3)+(\beta+u_{g(b)})x_{t,b}+\eta_{t,b},
\qquad u_g\sim N(0,\tau^2).
\]

The common slope is present only when the ordinary covariate term is included.
Otherwise the slopes are centred on zero. Positive and negative slopes are
both allowed. The residual matrix retains tinyAM's stationary age/year AR1:

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_{t,b},\eta_{s,c})=
\frac{\sigma_M^2\phi_A^{|b-c|}\phi_T^{|t-s|}}
     {(1-\phi_A^2)(1-\phi_T^2)}.
\]

Here \(\sigma_M\) is the existing innovation-scale SD. One slope is drawn per
group, independently of this residual process, and reused across all years.
The integrated log-mortality covariance is
\(\tau^2ZZ^\mathsf{T}+C_{\mathrm{AR1}}\), where each row of \(Z\) places that
year's covariate in its slope group's column. Repeating a biological age in
a shared M block does not add another process-density contribution.

## Study design

The tracked `m_random_slopes.R` script generates 40 years with eight groups,
four groups, or four groups with persistent covariates and residuals.
There are `r result$n_isolated` isolated and `r result$n_full` full-assessment
replicates per scenario. Seeds, configurations, warnings, errors and every
completed attempt are retained in the ignored results folder.
The reported run used R 4.4.1 and RTMB 2.0; numerical stopping behaviour can
vary between runtime versions.

True values are a common slope of −0.25, slope SD 0.15, M innovation SD 0.06,
age correlation 0.25 and year correlation 0.6 (0.9 in the persistent case).
Independent Normal covariates are used in the first two scenarios; the stress
case uses an AR1 covariate with correlation 0.95. Study covariates are explicitly
centred and standardized. The package never transforms user covariates this way.

The isolated study draws log mortality using an independently constructed
multivariate Normal covariance. It integrates the group slopes in RTMB and
estimates all five parameters. Deterministic tests independently verify the
Gaussian likelihood and derivatives.

The full assessments simulate recruitment, F, M, catch and two surveys at
different times of year. N has no additional cohort error; F has IID deviations
around age-specific means. Both observation log-SDs are supplied as 0.08.
Catch, recruitment, F, M, q and the mean/process parameters are then fitted.
Initial population and mortality states use the simulated states as favourable
starts. The common slope and slope effects start at zero, estimated process SDs
at 0.1, and M correlations at 0.3/0.5. This tests recovery with favourable starts,
not robustness to arbitrary starting values. No failed model is rescued or
retuned. Eight-group models contain 17 biological ages; four-group models
contain nine, demonstrating genuine within-block age sharing.
The study explicitly estimates M states from the first modeled year. The
package's default second-year M start is unchanged and tested separately.

## Numerical reliability

```{r numerical-table}
knitr::kable(performance, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Numerical success requires optimizer code zero, a positive-definite Hessian
and maximum absolute gradient at most 0.01. A missed gradient threshold is
reported separately from failures of uncertainty estimation. Every scheduled
replicate remains in the success-rate denominator, including errors.
The 90% benchmark applies to the well-informed eight-group scenario; it is a
reason to investigate failures, not a reason to change starts or tolerances.

The completed study had 100/100 numerical successes in each isolated scenario.
Full-assessment success was 12/30 with eight groups, 27/30 with four groups,
and 27/30 in the persistent scenario. Every full fit returned optimizer code
zero and a positive-definite Hessian. All 24 unsuccessful full fits missed the
gradient threshold; none were removed or rescued. The eight-group scenario
therefore **did not meet the 90% benchmark**, despite the exact Gaussian tests
and reliable isolated fits.

The first eight-group fit was examined without refitting. Its largest gradient
was 0.01870, on a catchability coefficient. Multiplying the gradient by the
estimated fixed-parameter covariance gave a maximum local displacement of
0.000133 standard errors. This suggests that optimizer stopping precision can
matter for this large model, but this one-fit check does not establish that
all missed thresholds are harmless. The fit remains classified as unsuccessful;
neither tolerances nor starting values were changed.

```{r success-figure}
groups <- split(runs, interaction(runs$scenario, runs$kind))
rates <- vapply(groups, function(x) mean(x$is_converged), numeric(1))
names(rates) <- vapply(groups, function(x) paste(label[x$scenario[1]], x$kind[1], sep = "\n"), character(1))
barplot(100 * rates, ylim = c(0, 100), las = 1, ylab = "Numerical success (%)",
  col = rep(c("#00475D", "#FF6B35"), each = 3), cex.names = .7)
abline(h = 90, lty = 2, col = "grey45")
```

## Parameter and mortality recovery

```{r recovery-table}
shown <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(summary, interaction(summary$scenario, summary$kind)), function(x) {
  values <- setNames(sprintf("%.3f (%.0f%%)", x$median, 100 * x$coverage), x$parameter)
  data.frame(Scenario = unname(label[x$scenario[1]]), Experiment = x$kind[1],
    Intervals = paste(range(x$intervals), collapse = "–"),
    `Common slope` = values["beta"], `Slope SD` = values["slope_sd"],
    `M innovation SD` = values["residual_sd"], `Age correlation` = values["phi_age"],
    `Year correlation` = values["phi_year"], check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(shown, row.names = FALSE)
```

Cells show the median estimate and, in parentheses, interval coverage.
Coverage is the proportion of available 95% intervals containing the generating
value; interval counts are shown explicitly. These intervals require a
positive-definite uncertainty calculation, but the table does not otherwise
filter out numerically unsuccessful fits. Point estimates use all finite
returned values. With only 30 full replicates, coverage estimates are imprecise.
Group-SD recovery is also limited by the number of groups, regardless of how
many ages are pooled within each one.

The full-assessment median slope SD was about 0.12 with eight groups and 0.11
with four groups (truth 0.15). Common-slope interval coverage was about 80%,
83% and 87% across the three scenarios. Isolated common-slope coverage was
88%, 77% and 83%, respectively. Thus numerically successful Gaussian fits do
not guarantee well-calibrated uncertainty with so few independent groups.

```{r parameter-figure}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(5, 4, 2, 1))
for (parameter in c("beta", "slope_sd", "residual_sd", "phi_age", "phi_year")) {
  d <- parameters[parameters$kind == "full" & parameters$parameter == parameter &
    is.finite(parameters$estimate), ]
  d$scenario <- factor(d$scenario, levels = names(label), labels = c("Eight\ngroups", "Four\ngroups", "Persistent"))
  title <- c(beta = "Common slope", slope_sd = "Slope SD", residual_sd = "M innovation SD",
    phi_age = "Age-block correlation", phi_year = "Year correlation")
  boxplot(estimate ~ scenario, d, main = title[parameter], xlab = "", ylab = "Estimate",
    log = if (parameter %in% c("slope_sd", "residual_sd")) "y" else "",
    col = "#8CC9C5", cex.axis = .8)
  if (parameter == "phi_year") points(1:3, c(.6, .6, .9), pch = 4, cex = 1.3)
  else abline(h = d$truth[1], lty = 2)
}
plot.new()
text(.5, .6, "Dashed lines / crosses: truth\nAll finite estimates retained\nSD panels use logarithmic axes", cex = .9)
```

```{r state-recovery}
state_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(result$results, function(x) {
  if (x$run$kind != "full" || is.null(x$slopes)) return(NULL)
  intervals <- is.finite(x$slopes$lower) & is.finite(x$slopes$upper) & isTRUE(x$diagnostics$pdHess)
  data.frame(scenario = x$run$scenario,
    slope_rmse = sqrt(mean((x$slopes$estimate - x$slopes$truth)^2)),
    log_M_rmse = sqrt(mean((x$mortality$estimate - x$mortality$truth)^2)),
    group_intervals = sum(intervals),
    group_covered = sum(x$slopes$lower[intervals] <= x$slopes$truth[intervals] &
      x$slopes$upper[intervals] >= x$slopes$truth[intervals]))
}))
state_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(state_summary, state_summary$scenario), function(x) {
  data.frame(Scenario = unname(label[x$scenario[1]]),
    `Median slope RMSE` = median(x$slope_rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Median log-M RMSE` = median(x$log_M_rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Group intervals` = sum(x$group_intervals),
    `Group coverage` = if (sum(x$group_intervals)) sum(x$group_covered) / sum(x$group_intervals) else NA_real_,
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(state_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Group-slope intervals describe the random deviations, not the sum of the
common and group slopes. Realized M recovery is evaluated on the log scale
using only unique fitted block states. No unsupported intervals are invented
for the combined M mean surface.

## Workflow validation

The first four-group replicate is used without selecting a better-fitting
example. Updates, forecast covariate handling, warm-start alignment,
retrospective/hindcast folds, signed effect intervals and a browser-free
dashboard are checked separately from recovery performance.

The one-year hindcast fold missed the gradient threshold (0.0142 versus 0.01).
Its forecast score was left unavailable.
This exposed an existing empty-forecast table error, now covered by a regression
test: missing forecasts return an unavailable score rather than a table-size
error. The projection update and historical retrospective fold completed.

```{r workflow-checks}
workflow_file <- "results/m_random_slopes/workflow_checks.csv"
if (file.exists(workflow_file)) {
  workflow <- read.csv(workflow_file)
  knitr::kable(workflow[c("check", "passed", "error")], row.names = FALSE)
} else cat("Workflow validation has not been run.\n")
```

## Interpretation and limits

This extension permits a valid model specification; it does not establish that
an age-specific food response is supported by a particular assessment. A common
fixed slope is the useful first comparison. Four groups provide little
information about the distribution of slopes. Persistent covariates and AR1
deviations can produce similar trajectories, and good mortality recovery does
not guarantee that their separate contributions have been recovered.
The full study uses known observation SDs and IID F deviations; it does not
establish recovery with additional N error, AR1 F deviations or time-varying q.

Retain this option for targeted sensitivity analyses, not routine interpretation
of food-response differences between four age groups. Check a common fixed
slope first, examine slope-SD and persistence intervals, and keep numerical
failures separate from evidence about the ecological hypothesis. No automatic
model simplification or rescue fitting is performed.

## Implementation checks

The focused tests passed 48 random-slope assertions and 32 hindcast-control
assertions. They cover block conflicts, the optional common slope, independently
calculated Gaussian densities and derivatives, unobserved forecast states,
simulation, warm-start alignment and uncertainty advisories. Existing mean and
process-SD regression tests also passed. The full package suite passed under
R 4.4.1 and R 4.6.1. Dashboard validation renders files without opening a browser.
`R CMD check --no-manual` passed with no errors, warnings or notes. The clean
source check used Pandoc explicitly; an earlier check could not find Pandoc,
and its dashboard-test failures were environmental rather than model failures.

The real Northern cod trial was **not run**: the local packaged data do not
contain `log_cap_per_cod`. `inst/examples/example_m_random_slopes.R` shows the
proposed comparison and stops until an actual covariate is supplied. It uses
that column as an external predictor; it does not recreate an official food
relationship by recomputing capelin per modeled cod.

Run the study from the repository root, then render this report. The rendered
HTML, figures, example fits, attempt tables and checkpoints belong under
`results/m_random_slopes/`, which is ignored. Scheduler interruptions, if any,
are logged separately from completed optimizer outcomes. Existing successes
and failures are reused when resuming the same study; use a fresh output folder
when changing the generating design.
